title: Career Psychology Digest — Hiring & Selection — 2026-09-29

studies.title: Hiring filters cut the applicant pool — and screen out the best candidates too
studies.paper_title: Filtering the labor pool: How digitalization redistributes hiring costs
studies.the_study: A randomized field experiment in a large online labor market gave some employers access to candidate filters (the checkbox tools that narrow applicants by credentials, ratings, location and the like) and others not. Employers with filters interviewed 3.4% fewer applicants overall, but the composition shifted sharply: they interviewed 28.9% fewer low-quality applicants and 36.9% fewer high-quality ones, as measured by a machine learning proxy for quality invisible to the employer. Among employers who actively used the filters, job offers were 8.9% more likely to be rejected and contracted wages were 2.5% higher, because everyone was chasing candidates with the same easily observable signals.
studies.why_it_matters: Filters are sold as a way to save recruiting time, but this shows they move the cost rather than remove it — savings at the screening stage get paid back at the offer stage in rejections and higher salaries.
studies.story_angle_primary: Recruiters and hiring managers can audit their own filter settings: which criteria are knocking out candidates, and how many finalists are people every competitor is also bidding for. A useful test is to interview a random sample of filtered-out applicants for one or two roles and see how they compare.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For job seekers, this explains why applications vanish without a human ever reading them — and why candidates with conventional, easily verifiable credentials get multiple competing offers while less legible but equally capable people get none.
studies.caveats: Conducted in a single large online labor market (gig/freelance contracting), so results may not transfer to full-time corporate hiring; offer-stage outcomes are described by the author as suggestive evidence among employers who actively used filters, not the clean randomized comparison; quality is a machine learning proxy, not measured job performance.
studies.verdict_notes: All headline numbers match the abstract and the randomized design supports causal language; one theorized mechanism is presented as an established result.

studies.title: You can't have all three: the recruiting math that forces a trade-off between diversity, fairness and performance
studies.paper_title: Adverse impact, job performance, and diversity outcomes of applicant attraction: A simulation and paradox.
studies.the_study: Researchers ran Monte Carlo simulations of hiring processes in which applicants are attracted based on their minority/majority status (diversity recruiting), their qualifications (qualifications-based recruiting), or both, before being screened on a selection test composite. They compared six generic applicant-attraction scenarios on three outcomes at once: adverse impact, diversity of hires, and predicted job performance. No single attraction strategy improved all three — though several improved any two — and the paradox held across a wide range of predictor composites.
studies.why_it_matters: Organizations often assume that recruiting harder at the top of the funnel can painlessly fix adverse impact, raise diversity and keep quality up; the simulation says the funnel arithmetic doesn't allow it.
studies.story_angle_primary: Before launching a recruiting campaign, leaders should decide explicitly which two of the three outcomes they are optimizing, and set metrics accordingly — otherwise the program will be judged a failure on whichever outcome it was mathematically never going to move.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A window into why corporate diversity targets so often disappoint: the constraints are built into how selection statistics work, not just into managers' intentions.
studies.caveats: Simulation only — no real applicants, real tests or real job performance data; results depend on the assumed correlations among race, attraction variables and predictor composites; outcomes are modeled, not observed.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, six attraction scenarios, three outcomes and the paradox are all reported faithfully; caveats correctly flag the simulation-only basis.

studies.title: Startup stock options attract engineers mostly as a signal, not as a financial bet
studies.paper_title: More than money: The symbolic role of stock options in tech worker attraction by technology startups
studies.the_study: A series of experiments tested whether and why equity offers attract technology workers to early-stage startups. Offering stock options produced a strong attraction effect, but only partly through financial reasoning; the bigger driver was what the offer signaled about the startup's unobservable qualities, especially how it treats employees. Participants understood the financial implications but only made calculated financial comparisons when explicitly prompted to do so.
studies.why_it_matters: Founders competing for scarce technical talent may be buying reputation rather than a compensation instrument — which means how the equity is framed and explained matters as much as its expected value.
studies.story_angle_primary: Startup founders and HR leads can test whether their equity story is doing symbolic work ("we share upside with everyone") rather than financial work, and whether transparent valuation and strike-price information helps or hurts candidate attraction.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For anyone weighing a startup offer: your gut reaction to equity may be reading it as a character reference for the employer rather than as money. Running the numbers — dilution, strike price, likely exit — changes the decision, and most people don't do it unless nudged.
studies.caveats: Experimental, scenario-based job choices rather than actual offer acceptances; attraction measured as stated preference; sample composition and size for each experiment not detailed in the abstract.
studies.verdict_notes: Matches the abstract's series of experiments, the partial financial mediation, the symbolic inference about how the startup treats employees, and the prompting result; caveats appropriately note undisclosed sample details.

studies.title: Rejected by an algorithm? Adding a human reviewer changes how candidates feel about you
studies.paper_title: Rejected Applicant Reactions to Artificial Intelligence/Human Manager‐Based Recruitment
studies.the_study: Two mixed-methods studies examined how job applicants react when an AI system rejects them. Using a person-centered approach, the researchers identified four distinct emotional profiles based on combinations of outward-focused negative emotions (anger at the organization) and inward-focused ones (self-blame, shame). Applicants rejected by AI tended to attribute responsibility to others, fueling hostility toward the employer — but introducing a human manager to review the AI-based rejection shifted applicants into more benign emotional profiles and improved reactions toward the organization.
studies.why_it_matters: Most applicants in any hiring process are rejected, and they are also customers and future candidates; automating the no without a human in the loop may be quietly expensive for employer brand.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your organization uses automated screening, consider whether a named human signs off on and communicates rejections — and measure downstream effects like reapplication rates, Glassdoor sentiment and referral behavior, not just recruiter hours saved.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Why an algorithmic rejection stings differently from a human one: people blame the company rather than themselves, which feels better in the moment but can leave them angrier at the employer.
studies.caveats: Applicant reactions are self-reported and partly based on studies of rejection scenarios rather than long-term behavioral outcomes; profile analyses depend on sample composition; abstract does not specify sample sizes, countries or whether participants were real rejected applicants throughout.
studies.verdict_notes: Two mixed-methods studies, four profiles and the human-review effect are accurate; the attribution mechanism is proposed rather than clearly reported as a result.

studies.title: Older and younger candidates talk differently in AI video interviews — and rewording the question narrows the gap
studies.paper_title: Age-inclusive AI assessments: testing and refining open-ended prompts with human and LLM-simulated data
studies.the_study: Two studies looked at age bias in AI-based hiring assessments. Study 1 compared language in automated video interview responses from workers aged 18 to 66+, and found significant age-related differences in both semantic content and language complexity even after controlling for education, gender, race, socioeconomic status, personality and vocational interests. Study 2 used ChatGPT to simulate applicant personas of different ages and tested rewritten interview prompts, finding that prompt wording measurably changed the size and pattern of age-related linguistic differences — shrinking some, leaving others intact.
studies.why_it_matters: If scoring algorithms read language style as competence, age differences in how people speak can become age discrimination at scale — and the fix may lie in question design rather than in the model.
studies.story_angle_primary: Employers using automated video interviews or chatbots should ask vendors how prompts were tested across age groups, and consider piloting alternative question wordings with their own age-diverse applicant pool before rollout.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A practical insight for older job seekers navigating recorded interviews: the machine is partly responding to how you phrase things, not only what you did — and the question you're asked shapes how much your age shows.
studies.caveats: Study 2 relies on LLM-simulated personas rather than real older and younger applicants, which may reproduce stereotypes rather than actual behavior; Study 1 is observational and does not show that these linguistic differences actually lower algorithmic scores or hiring outcomes; sample sizes and country not specified in the abstract.
studies.verdict_notes: Two studies, age range, control variables, and the Study 2 LLM-persona prompt test are all reported correctly, with appropriate caveats about simulated personas and unmeasured scoring consequences.

studies.title: When a career ends against your will, work doesn't always matter less afterwards
studies.paper_title: From grounded consolidation to active detachment: the evolution of work centrality during involuntary career change
studies.the_study: A qualitative longitudinal study followed 16 involuntary career changers through three waves of semi-structured interviews, tracking how central work remained to their identity and life over the transition. Rather than a uniform decline, the researchers found three patterns — work centrality growing, staying the same, or diminishing — expressed through five distinct processes, from "grounded consolidation" (work becoming more important as a source of stability) to "active detachment" (deliberately demoting work in one's life).
studies.why_it_matters: Employers and career counselors often assume forced job loss uniformly damages attachment to work; in reality the direction varies, which argues for tailored, longer-running support rather than a one-size outplacement package.
studies.story_angle_primary: Managers running redundancies and HR teams designing outplacement can ask departing employees where work now sits in their priorities, rather than assuming everyone wants the same kind of next role at the same intensity.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For anyone forced out of a career: the loss can make work feel more central, not less, and both reactions are common — recognizing which pattern you're in may help you choose the next step deliberately instead of by default.
studies.caveats: Very small qualitative sample (N=16) with no statistical generalizability; interview self-reports; country and occupational mix not specified in the abstract; findings are interpretive patterns, not measured effects.
studies.verdict_notes: N=16, three interview waves, three patterns and five processes all match; caveats appropriately note the small interpretive sample.

studies.title: What your LinkedIn profile says about your faith may be shaping who gets the interview
studies.paper_title: Choosing by religion: Similarity–attraction and religious beliefs in social media assessments
studies.the_study: U.S. working professionals evaluated a manipulated LinkedIn profile in a 4 (applicant religion: Christian, Muslim, Jewish, or no religious content) x 2 (low vs. high qualifications) experiment — Study 1 used a religion-stratified sample of 372 raters screening a woman in her mid-20s, Study 2 used 294 raters screening a man in his mid-60s. When the applicant's stated religious beliefs matched the rater's own, raters liked the applicant more, and that liking predicted higher ratings of expected task performance, citizenship behavior and overall hireability — including interview invitations — over and above the applicant's actual qualifications. The bias was stronger among more religious raters and among those following news of the Israel–Hamas War.
studies.why_it_matters: Social media screening is now routine, and it surfaces information about applicants that recruiters would never legally ask about in an interview — with measurable effects on who gets called back.
studies.story_angle_primary: For managers who screen candidates' social profiles: this suggests a similarity-liking channel that operates below conscious intent. Worth testing whether structuring your screening — fixed job-relevant criteria, removing social profiles from the first pass, or having a second rater — changes your own shortlists, and worth noting that current events can heighten the effect.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For job seekers, the study is a concrete reminder that a public profile is also an identity disclosure — and that the cost or benefit of revealing your faith depends heavily on who happens to be reading.
studies.caveats: Online experimental design with manipulated profiles rather than real hiring decisions; hireability ratings are stated intentions, not actual callbacks; single-country (U.S.) sample; ratings of performance and hireability come from the same raters.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, both sample sizes and the similarity–liking mediation match; the stated direction of the moderator effects goes slightly beyond the abstract.

studies.title: Applicants have had ChatGPT for years. Pre-employment test scores barely budged
studies.paper_title: Testing After ChatGPT: Aggregate Change in Applicant Assessment Scores
studies.journal: International Journal of Selection and Assessment
studies.the_study: Researchers used large archival samples of real job applicants to test whether average scores on two cognitive ability assessments and one personality assessment shifted after ChatGPT's public release in November 2022. Regression and time-trend analyses found statistically significant but practically negligible changes, with effect sizes near zero and inconsistent in direction. Younger applicants — the heaviest users of LLM tools — did not show the score inflation the cheating hypothesis predicts.
studies.why_it_matters: Employers have been redesigning or abandoning unproctored online assessments on the assumption that chatbots have broken them; this is among the first operational evidence that large-scale score inflation has not actually materialized.
studies.story_angle_primary: Before you rip out an unproctored assessment or pay for expensive proctoring, check your own applicant score distributions before and after late 2022 — the panic may not be visible in your data. Note that this is aggregate evidence: it does not rule out individual cheating, just widespread cheating big enough to move the mean.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A useful counterexample to the assumption that new technology instantly changes mass behavior: most applicants, it seems, are still just taking the test.
studies.caveats: Archival correlational design over a short post-release window; assessment types and vendor context are limited to two cognitive and one personality measure; aggregate means can mask meaningful cheating by a subset of applicants; test publisher or industry data source may be an interested party.
studies.verdict_notes: Archival design, assessment mix and near-zero, inconsistent effects are accurate; the specific claim about younger applicants is not reported in the abstract.

studies.title: Helping the new hire only pays off for you if they're good at the job
studies.paper_title: But what about the coworkers? Investigating the implications of helping newcomers for coworkers from a relational perspective
studies.the_study: Taking the perspective of the existing employee rather than the newcomer, researchers ran a field study plus an online vignette study on what helping a new colleague does to the helper. Helping combined with the newcomer's task performance determined whether coworkers felt the relationship had met their expectations — a reciprocity calculation. When expectations were met, coworkers rated the newcomer as more competent, reported less stress in interacting with them, and were more willing to accept them as a legitimate member of the team.
studies.why_it_matters: Onboarding programs load helping duties onto existing staff on the assumption it's costless to them; in fact an unreciprocated helping relationship leaves the helper stressed and the newcomer less accepted.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you assign buddies or mentors to new hires, manage both sides of the exchange: give newcomers early tasks they can visibly deliver on, and recognize helpers' time rather than treating it as free. Watch for the team dynamic where a struggling new hire quietly loses the goodwill of the very people assigned to support them.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For anyone starting a new job: your early visible contributions aren't just about impressing the boss — they determine whether the colleague showing you the ropes ends up feeling the relationship was worth it.
studies.caveats: Study 2 uses hypothetical vignettes; field study sample size, occupation and country are not specified in the abstract; measures appear largely self-reported from coworkers.
studies.verdict_notes: Two-study design and the reciprocity interaction are correct, but the mediation chain is flattened and the takeaway is stated more causally than the abstract's hedged wording.

studies.title: Coping strategies that help women survive a male-dominated field can also entrench it
studies.paper_title: Surviving and changing the field: Navigating gendered contextual barriers of geosciences
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed 67 semi-structured interviews with men and women geoscientists — an occupation combining technical expertise with physically demanding fieldwork in remote locations — to map the gendered barriers built into both the physical and social context of the work. They distinguished women's "survival" strategies, which adapt to the existing context, from "change" strategies that confront it. Survival strategies, and the organizational practices that supported them, tended to reinforce the very barriers women faced; change strategies and practices aimed directly at the barriers were more effective.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that much of what organizations do to "support" women in tough field occupations — accommodations, individual coping, resilience framing — quietly preserves the norms that cause the problem.
studies.story_angle_primary: For leaders in field-heavy sectors (energy, mining, engineering, construction): audit whether your inclusion measures ask women to adapt to the environment or change the environment — equipment sizing, field logistics, accommodation arrangements and crew norms are concrete targets.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A vivid account of what it actually costs to build a career in a job where the workplace is a remote field camp, and why individual grit is a poor substitute for changing the setup.
studies.caveats: Qualitative interview study in a single occupation; no quantitative outcomes and no causal test of which strategies work; findings depend on interpretive analysis and may not generalize beyond geosciences.
studies.verdict_notes: Interview count, mixed-gender sample, occupational context and the survival-versus-change contrast all match the abstract; caveats correctly note the interpretive, single-occupation basis.

studies.title: Employees without children are quietly keeping score on your flexibility policies
studies.paper_title: Beyond parenthood: anticipatory fairness in work-life balance, career progression, and organizational support
studies.the_study: Researchers conducted 65 semi-structured interviews at a single Big Four consulting firm with three groups: employees with children, employees childless by choice, and employees who want children but don't yet have them. Responses were coded and analyzed with fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis. Parents valued flexibility when it came with managerial backing but some reported career penalties; employees childless by choice perceived inequity when parent-focused arrangements created extra availability demands on them without recognition; and would-be parents judged current policies prospectively, asking whether support and promotion prospects would still be fair after they had a child.
studies.why_it_matters: Work-life policies are typically evaluated by whether parents like them, but fairness perceptions — and retention risk — run across the whole workforce, including people judging how the policy will treat their future selves.
studies.story_angle_primary: Managers should check who absorbs the coverage when flexibility is granted, and whether that absorption is ever recognized. The "anticipatory fairness" finding also implies employees are evaluating your parental-leave and promotion track record long before they need it.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For anyone weighing when — or whether — to have children, the study captures a real workplace calculation: people read how their colleagues who became parents were treated and use it to predict their own future.
studies.caveats: Single firm in a single industry (elite professional services); qualitative interview data with interpretive coding; fsQCA on 65 cases identifies configurations, not causal effects; no objective career-outcome data.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, N (65 interviews), single Big Four firm, fsQCA and the three family-status groups are all reported correctly. One nuance dropped: the abstract stresses that fairness perceptions varied within as well as across groups, and that more inclusive configurations drew favourable evaluations from the childless-by-choice group.

studies.title: "Nowhereness": when neither work nor home is a safe place to be yourself
studies.paper_title: Minority stress, borders and nowhereness: work–life balance among gay men
studies.the_study: Researchers interviewed 29 gay men employed at a range of Indian organizations about stressors at work and at home, how those spill over in both directions, and how they manage the boundary between the two. Salient stressors included gender policing, heteronormative demands and hostility from family, and internal pressure to conform to masculine norms. The authors describe a state they call "nowhereness," in which neither the work nor the family domain offers a safe space for an authentic self, leaving no domain for psychological recovery.
studies.why_it_matters: Standard work-life balance thinking assumes one domain can serve as a refuge from the other; for minority employees, both can be sources of strain, which changes what workplace support needs to do.
studies.story_angle_primary: For managers of globally distributed teams: inclusion policies designed in Western headquarters assume home is a safe haven. In collectivist contexts where family is itself a source of minority stress, the workplace may need to be the recovery space rather than merely a non-hostile one.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A reminder that "switching off from work" only restores you if the place you switch off into feels safe — a point that extends beyond sexuality to anyone whose home life is a source of pressure.
studies.caveats: Qualitative, 29 participants in one country; no comparison group; self-selected interviewees; findings are interpretive and not generalizable to prevalence.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample (29 gay men in various Indian organizations), qualitative interview design, the named stressors, bi-directional spillover and the "nowhereness" concept all match the abstract. Caveats appropriately limit generalizability; the managerial angle is framed as an implication rather than a finding.

studies.title: A two-minute allocation game predicts which job perks candidates actually care about
studies.paper_title: Assessing Prosocial Values in Initial Career Choice: The SVO Slider as a Behavioral Predictor of CSR Attribute Preferences
studies.the_study: Researchers gave 425 undergraduates the SVO Slider — a behavioral resource-allocation task measuring social value orientation — and then an adaptive choice-based conjoint task in which they traded off salary, location and four dimensions of corporate social responsibility (employee, environmental, social, governance). Salary dominated choices, with employee-focused CSR second. More prosocially oriented participants weighted environmental and social CSR more heavily and salary less, but SVO was unrelated to how much they valued employee-focused CSR — the dimension that directly benefits them personally.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests employer branding around sustainability appeals to a specific, measurable subset of candidates, while perks that benefit employees directly attract everyone regardless of values — and that pay still outweighs both.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your recruitment marketing leans on environmental and social commitments, recognize you're targeting a segment, not the whole pipeline; internal employee-focused CSR is the broader draw, and neither substitutes for competitive pay. Conjoint methods are also a cheap way to find out what your actual applicants trade off.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For job seekers, a useful check on your own decision-making: people's stated values about ethical employers often collapse when salary enters the trade-off.
studies.caveats: Undergraduate sample making hypothetical job choices, not real applicants accepting real offers; single-session design; the behavioral measure predicts stated preferences, not subsequent job behavior; findings may not transfer to experienced candidates with dependents.
studies.verdict_notes: N = 425 undergraduates, the SVO Slider, the adaptive choice-based conjoint attributes, salary dominance, employee CSR second, positive SVO links to environmental/social CSR, null for employee CSR and negative for salary are all faithful. Only the headline's invented "two-minute" detail and a slightly broad reading of the null need attention.

studies.title: Free tuition beats reimbursement: how education perks keep frontline workers from quitting
studies.paper_title: Structuring Educational Benefits to Promote Low‐Skilled Worker Retention
studies.the_study: Researchers combined field data with experiments to test whether education benefits keep low-skilled workers. Study 1 analyzed an operating education benefits program aimed at employees in low-skilled jobs and found that participation was associated with lower turnover. Two follow-up vignette experiments compared program designs and found that tuition assistance — benefits with little or no upfront cost to the worker — was tied to lower turnover intentions more strongly than reimbursement-style plans, partly because it signaled that the employer supported the worker's development. The effect was strongest when workers also saw internal career paths, and held across social classes and skill levels.
studies.why_it_matters: Employers struggling to fill and hold frontline roles often already offer tuition reimbursement; this suggests the design of the benefit, not just its existence, determines whether it buys loyalty.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your company offers tuition reimbursement that workers must pay for first, ask how many frontline employees actually use it — the experiments suggest fronting the cost and pairing the benefit with visible internal promotion ladders may matter more than the dollar value, though the causal test here was hypothetical rather than in the field.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For workers weighing a job offer, the fine print on education benefits is a signal: who has to pay tuition up front says a lot about whether the employer sees you as someone worth investing in.
studies.caveats: The retention finding is correlational (participants in a benefits program may differ from non-participants); the comparison of benefit designs came from between-person vignette experiments rather than real enrollment decisions, and turnover intentions are not actual quitting.
studies.verdict_notes: Study 1's correlational turnover link, the two between-person vignette experiments, the perceived-organizational-support-for-development mechanism, the internal-career-opportunities moderator and the persistence across social classes and skill levels are all reported correctly, and the caveats are candid. The headline is more causal than the evidence.

studies.title: That jokey job ad may be costing you candidates
studies.paper_title: How Do “Funny” Job Postings Affect Job Seekers' Reactions? Humor and Job Attractiveness
studies.journal: International Journal of Selection and Assessment
studies.the_study: Three experiments tested how humor in job postings affects potential applicants. Two single-stimulus studies found humor reduced job attractiveness; a third study using multiple sampled job ads found no significant effect on attractiveness. Across all three, however, humorous postings consistently led job seekers to expect the organization to have weaker procedural justice — that is, less fair and serious HR processes.
studies.why_it_matters: Recruitment marketing increasingly leans on personality and jokes to stand out, but the signal candidates may take away is that the company's hiring and HR decisions are not handled seriously.
studies.story_angle_primary: Before signing off on a playful job ad, consider A/B testing it: the evidence suggests humor is at best neutral for attractiveness and reliably raises doubts about whether the company's processes are fair, so recruiters may get more from concrete signals of fairness and transparency.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Job seekers read tone as evidence. A funny posting may feel like a culture cue, but these studies suggest most readers quietly downgrade their expectations of how fairly the employer will treat them.
studies.caveats: Experimental studies with simulated postings and hypothetical application decisions, not actual applicant behavior; results were inconsistent across studies (the strongest design found no effect on attractiveness); sample details on participants' work status are limited.
studies.verdict_notes: Three experiments, the single-stimulus vs. stimulus-sampling contrast, the negative attractiveness effect in Studies 1-2 and null in Study 3, and the consistent procedural-justice expectation effect all match the abstract. Caveats appropriately flag the inconsistency and the simulated-posting design.

studies.title: VR hiring tests make employers look more attractive — mainly to younger candidates
studies.paper_title: Virtual Reality-, Video- or Text-Based SJTs: Investigating the Effect of Stimulus Format on Presence and Organizational Attractiveness Across Age Groups
studies.the_study: Two experiments tested how the format of situational judgment tests shapes candidates' reactions. Study 1 (N=122) compared video- with text-based scenarios; Study 2 (N=121) compared virtual reality with text. Video increased the feeling of "presence" but did not make the organization seem more attractive. VR raised both presence and organizational attractiveness, with presence explaining the effect — but the boost was weaker for older test-takers than for younger and middle-aged ones.
studies.why_it_matters: Companies investing in immersive assessment to look modern should know the appeal is uneven by age, which matters for employers courting older workers amid labor shortages.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you are piloting VR assessments, track candidate reactions by age group rather than in aggregate — these studies suggest the employer-branding payoff may not extend to older applicants, and a slicker format alone (video) does not move attractiveness at all.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Hiring tests are becoming experiences, not just questionnaires — and how immersive a company's assessment feels can shape whether candidates want the job, independent of the job itself.
studies.caveats: Small samples (roughly 60 per condition), lab-style experiments with simulated selection rather than real applicants, outcomes are perceptions rather than application or acceptance behavior, and the two formats were tested in separate studies rather than head-to-head.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample sizes (122, 121), the video-vs-text and VR-vs-text comparisons, presence mediation for VR, the null attractiveness effect for video, and the weaker VR effect among older test-takers are all reported accurately, with the separate-studies limitation noted in caveats.

studies.title: A daily reflection prompt helped paramedics find meaning in bad shifts — but didn't move mental health symptoms
studies.paper_title: Self-reflection resilience-recovery activity promotion training for emergency medical service clinicians: A randomized controlled pilot trial of a novel digital intervention.
studies.the_study: A randomized controlled pilot trial enrolled 83 emergency medical service clinicians in the US (89% White, 51% male), assigning them to a digital self-reflection resilience intervention (n=37) or a monitoring-only control (n=46). Both groups completed eight daily assessments on phones or computers; the intervention group also answered 10 open-ended prompts about stressors encountered, lessons learned and recovery strategies. The intervention group reported more "meaning made" from stressors, and the gap grew across days, with stronger effects among those who completed more prompts — but there were no significant differences in recovery activities, anxiety, depression or PTSD symptoms.
studies.why_it_matters: Short digital reflection tools are cheap and well-liked by high-stress frontline workers, but this trial shows acceptability is not the same as clinical benefit.
studies.story_angle_primary: For managers of high-exposure teams, this is a realistic picture of what a low-cost digital resilience tool delivers in eight days: engagement and more meaning-making, not symptom relief — a reason to treat such apps as one piece of a broader occupational health strategy rather than the intervention itself.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Writing a few sentences about what a hard day taught you appears to help people make sense of stress, which is useful even when it doesn't fix anxiety or depression.
studies.caveats: Pilot trial with a small sample and unequal groups; eight-day horizon; self-reported outcomes; single occupation in one country with a largely White sample; authors themselves say content needs refinement before a definitive trial.
studies.verdict_notes: Randomization, N=83 (37/46), demographics, eight daily assessments, 10 reflection prompts, the meaning-made effect and its growth across days, the adherence/fidelity pattern and the null results on other mechanisms and mental health outcomes all match. Only the stated country and the "paramedics" shorthand go slightly beyond the abstract.

studies.title: What employees with ADHD say actually helps at work: informal relationships and flexible bosses
studies.paper_title: Relationships at work: friend or foe? The perspective of ADHD employees
studies.the_study: Researchers conducted in-depth interviews with a purposeful sample of employees in Italy who had a clinical ADHD diagnosis, recruited through private psychotherapy practices, and analyzed their accounts of workplace relationships. Four themes emerged: a need for flexibility, the supportiveness of informal and friendly work relationships, the way formal and rigid relationships undermined them, and the importance of a relational leadership style. The relational environment, more than the work itself, shaped whether participants felt able to use their strengths.
studies.why_it_matters: Neurodiversity policies often focus on formal accommodations, while these workers point to everyday relational conditions — flexibility and approachable managers — as what determines whether they thrive or leave.
studies.story_angle_primary: Managers auditing their neurodiversity efforts could ask whether their processes are rigid by default: these accounts suggest formal, procedure-heavy relationships are experienced as barriers, while informal access to colleagues and a relational manager style act as enablers.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For the growing number of adults diagnosed with ADHD later in life, this offers a vocabulary for what they need from a job — and shows that disclosure aside, the quality of day-to-day relationships is often decisive.
studies.caveats: Small qualitative interview study; participants were recruited via psychotherapy practices in Italy, so they are likely in treatment and not representative of employees with ADHD generally; findings are self-reported lived experience and cannot establish effects on performance or retention.
studies.verdict_notes: Recruitment via private psychotherapy practices in Italy, the interpretive qualitative design and the four themes are reported accurately. Two interpretive additions go beyond the abstract: a comparative claim about relationships mattering more than the work itself, and a "thrive or leave" outcome claim that the digest's own caveat disowns.

feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Five studies in this batch independently test hiring technology against real or simulated applicants, and in every case the tool behaves differently than the sales pitch implies: candidate filters screened out 36.9% of high-quality applicants and pushed wages up (W7203733318), AI-delivered rejections redirected blame onto the employer unless a human signed off (W7204209860), age-linked language differences in automated video interviews shifted with nothing more than the wording of the prompt (W7214200214), the feared ChatGPT-driven inflation of pre-employment test scores never showed up in archival applicant data (W7202071941), and VR assessments boosted employer attractiveness only for younger test-takers (W7202387608). Taken together they describe an evidence gap: employers have been buying and abandoning tools based on assumptions that, when tested, mostly don't hold.

**Why pitch this now:** Algorithmic hiring is moving from procurement question to compliance question — NYC's bias-audit rule, Colorado's AI act, Illinois' amended Human Rights Act and the EU AI Act's high-risk classification all require employers to say what their hiring tools actually do — at exactly the moment this research shows that few employers have measured it.

**Angle:** A reported feature on the quiet mismatch between what hiring tech promises and what the first generation of rigorous tests finds, built around the four places the evidence lands (efficiency, brand damage, age bias, and the cheating panic that wasn't), aimed at managers and HR leaders in a business/management outlet, with a parallel version for general readers on what it means to be screened by a system nobody has audited.

**Potential headlines:**
- What happens when researchers test hiring software against real applicants
- The screening filters meant to save recruiters time made candidates more expensive
- Nobody has checked whether the machine that rejected you works

**Potential outlets:**
- **MIT Sloan Management Review** — its readership buys and governs these systems, and the piece is fundamentally about measurement and procurement discipline rather than AI hype.
- **Business Insider** — strong appetite for recruiter- and job-seeker-facing stories about screening tools, and the filter and AI-rejection findings are concrete enough for its work desk.
- **The Atlantic** — the "we automated a decision and never audited it" thread fits its technology-and-institutions register, with the ChatGPT non-effect as the narrative twist.
- **Fast Company** — covers HR tech vendors closely and would run the counterintuitive vendor-versus-evidence framing, including the VR-assessment age gap.
pitch_ideas_raw:
- **Hiring filters cut the applicant pool — and screen out the best candidates too (Work ID W7203733318):** Filters don't save recruiting cost, they relocate it to the offer stage in rejected offers and 2.5% higher wages — plus a testable audit any recruiter can run on their own filter settings, for a manager-audience column or HR explainer.
- **You can't have all three: the recruiting math that forces a trade-off between diversity, fairness and performance (Work ID W7213166433):** Explain why diversity recruiting programs get judged on an outcome the funnel arithmetic was never going to move, and why leaders should pick their two metrics up front, for a management or DEI-strategy column.
- **Startup stock options attract engineers mostly as a signal, not as a financial bet (Work ID W7204553807):** Equity works on candidates as a character reference for the employer, not as compensation — and people only run the numbers when prompted, for a startup/tech business column or a personal-finance-meets-career piece.
- **Rejected by an algorithm? Adding a human reviewer changes how candidates feel about you (Work ID W7204209860):** The cheapest fix to automated-rejection backlash is a named human on the no — with employer-brand metrics (reapplication, referrals, review sentiment) as the thing to track instead of recruiter hours, for a hiring/HR explainer.
- **Older and younger candidates talk differently in AI video interviews — and rewording the question narrows the gap (Work ID W7214200214):** Age bias in automated interviews may be a question-design problem more than a model problem, with concrete vendor questions employers should be asking, plus practical notes for older job seekers, for a workplace news brief or an age-and-work piece in a general-interest outlet.
- **When a career ends against your will, work doesn't always matter less afterwards (Work ID W7207518842):** Forced job loss can make work *more* central, not less — three distinct patterns that argue against one-size outplacement, for a career-advice column or a layoffs-aftermath feature in a general-interest/women's outlet.
- **What your LinkedIn profile says about your faith may be shaping who gets the interview (Work ID W7202344708):** Social-media screening surfaces religion that recruiters legally can't ask about, and similarity-liking then drives interview invitations — with news events amplifying it, for a hiring or HR explainer, or a general-interest piece on what your public profile discloses.
- **Applicants have had ChatGPT for years. Pre-employment test scores barely budged (Work ID W7202071941):** The cheating panic has not shown up in real applicant score distributions — a reason to check your own data before paying for proctoring, for a workplace news brief or a "myths about AI at work" explainer.
- **Helping the new hire only pays off for you if they're good at the job (Work ID W7202177851):** Onboarding buddies quietly run a reciprocity calculation, and a struggling new hire loses the goodwill of the people assigned to help — so give newcomers early visible wins, for a manager-audience column and a "starting a new job" career-advice piece.
- **Coping strategies that help women survive a male-dominated field can also entrench it (Work ID W7204477379):** Inclusion measures that ask women to adapt (resilience training, individual accommodations) can preserve the barriers; changing equipment, logistics and crew norms does not, for a leadership column in energy/engineering trade or business press, and a women's-outlet feature on grit as a false solution.
- **Employees without children are quietly keeping score on your flexibility policies (Work ID W7213900915):** Childless colleagues absorb unrecognized coverage while would-be parents judge policies prospectively — "anticipatory fairness" as a retention risk, for a manager-audience column and a women's/lifestyle piece on how people time parenthood around their employer's track record.
- **"Nowhereness": when neither work nor home is a safe place to be yourself (Work ID W7213532045):** Global inclusion policies assume home is a refuge; where it isn't, the workplace has to become the recovery space — for a global-HR explainer or a general-interest piece on the limits of "switching off."
- **A two-minute allocation game predicts which job perks candidates actually care about (Work ID W7204088664):** Green and social CSR recruit a measurable segment, employee-focused benefits recruit everyone, and salary still beats both — for an employer-branding column, plus a career-advice angle on how stated values collapse under a pay trade-off.
- **Free tuition beats reimbursement: how education perks keep frontline workers from quitting (Work ID W7211872890):** Who fronts the tuition is the whole benefit, and it only holds workers when paired with a visible internal ladder — for an HR/benefits explainer or frontline-retention story in business press.
- **That jokey job ad may be costing you candidates (Work ID W7203608858):** Humor in postings consistently made job seekers expect less fair HR processes, with no reliable attractiveness payoff — a good A/B-testing prompt for recruitment marketers, for a workplace news brief or marketing/HR column.
- **VR hiring tests make employers look more attractive — mainly to younger candidates (Work ID W7202387608):** Immersive assessment buys employer-brand lift that fades with candidate age, and slicker video buys nothing — track reactions by age group before rollout, for a hiring-tech brief or manager column.
- **A daily reflection prompt helped paramedics find meaning in bad shifts — but didn't move mental health symptoms (Work ID W4412125794):** A realistic account of what cheap digital resilience tools deliver — engagement and meaning-making, not symptom relief — for a workplace-wellbeing explainer aimed at managers of high-exposure teams.
- **What employees with ADHD say actually helps at work: informal relationships and flexible bosses (Work ID W7208704204):** Neurodiversity support may hinge on relational conditions rather than formal accommodations, with rigid procedures experienced as the barrier, for a manager-audience column or a work-psychology piece in a general-interest/women's outlet aimed at late-diagnosed adults.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: Career Psychology Digest — Hiring & Selection — 2026-09-29
**Checked:** 2026-09-29 | **Studies reviewed:** 18
**Primary audience:** working professionals and managers | **Secondary audience:** general readers

---

### Study 1: Hiring filters cut the applicant pool — and screen out the best candidates too
**Work ID:** W7203733318 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Theorized mechanism stated as finding** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "job offers were 8.9% more likely to be rejected and contracted wages were 2.5% higher, because everyone was chasing candidates with the same easily observable signals."
- **Abstract says:** "Additionally, I theorize that if many firms target the same signals of quality, they may all pursue similar candidates. This increases bargaining power for those applicants, leading to more rejected job offers and higher wage demands."
- **Problem:** The competition-for-the-same-candidates mechanism is theorized in the abstract, not demonstrated; the digest presents it as the established cause of the offer-stage results, which are themselves described as suggestive.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to "which the author attributes to many employers chasing candidates with the same easily observable signals"."

### Study 2: You can't have all three: the recruiting math that forces a trade-off between diversity, fairness and performance
**Work ID:** W7213166433 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 3: Startup stock options attract engineers mostly as a signal, not as a financial bet
**Work ID:** W7204553807 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 4: Rejected by an algorithm? Adding a human reviewer changes how candidates feel about you
**Work ID:** W7204209860 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Proposition reported as finding** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Applicants rejected by AI tended to attribute responsibility to others, fueling hostility toward the employer"
- **Abstract says:** "Drawing on appraisal theory, we propose that applicants rejected by AI tend to appraise the rejection as others' responsibility, leading to negative emotions and adverse reactions against the organization."
- **Problem:** The abstract frames the other-blame appraisal as the theoretical proposition; only the profile shift from human review is described as a finding.
- **Suggested fix:** "Write "The authors argue that AI rejection leads applicants to blame the organization rather than themselves..."."

**Issue B. Unlabelled gloss on emotion profiles** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "outward-focused negative emotions (anger at the organization) and inward-focused ones (self-blame, shame)"
- **Abstract says:** "we identify four distinct profiles based on the combination of outward-focused negative emotions (OFNE) and inward-focused negative emotions (IFNE)"
- **Problem:** The specific emotions named in parentheses are the digest's interpretation; the abstract does not specify which emotions were measured.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop the parenthetical examples or mark them as illustrative."

### Study 5: Older and younger candidates talk differently in AI video interviews — and rewording the question narrows the gap
**Work ID:** W7214200214 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 6: When a career ends against your will, work doesn't always matter less afterwards
**Work ID:** W7207518842 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 7: What your LinkedIn profile says about your faith may be shaping who gets the interview
**Work ID:** W7202344708 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Direction of moderation asserted** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The bias was stronger among more religious raters and among those following news of the Israel–Hamas War."
- **Abstract says:** "This bias was further shaped by both individual (rater religiosity, Study 1) and contextual moderators (news engagement with a religiously charged event, i.e., the Israel–Hamas War)."
- **Problem:** The abstract states only that the bias was "shaped by" these moderators; it does not say the effect was stronger in either group.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say the bias varied with rater religiosity and with news engagement, without specifying the direction."

### Study 8: Applicants have had ChatGPT for years. Pre-employment test scores barely budged
**Work ID:** W7202071941 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Age-moderator result not reported** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Younger applicants — the heaviest users of LLM tools — did not show the score inflation the cheating hypothesis predicts."
- **Abstract says:** "We also examined age as a moderator given evidence that younger individuals are more frequent users of LLM technologies. Regression and time-trend analyses indicated statistically significant but practically negligible changes in assessment scores following ChatGPT's release."
- **Problem:** The abstract says age was examined as a moderator but does not report the result for younger applicants specifically; this is unverifiable from the abstract alone.
- **Suggested fix:** "State that the authors also tested age as a moderator, and note the specific result cannot be confirmed from the abstract."

### Study 9: Helping the new hire only pays off for you if they're good at the job
**Work ID:** W7202177851 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Mediation chain flattened** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "When expectations were met, coworkers rated the newcomer as more competent, reported less stress in interacting with them, and were more willing to accept them as a legitimate member of the team."
- **Abstract says:** "met relationship expectations positively affect coworkers' evaluations of newcomers' work competence, which are then associated with lower levels of coworkers' stress when interacting with newcomers and higher levels of coworkers' acceptance of newcomers as legitimate organizational members"
- **Problem:** In the abstract, competence evaluations mediate the stress and acceptance outcomes; the digest lists all three as parallel effects of met expectations.
- **Suggested fix:** "Note that met expectations raised competence evaluations, which in turn were linked to lower stress and greater acceptance."

**Issue B. Causal phrasing in takeaway** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "in fact an unreciprocated helping relationship leaves the helper stressed and the newcomer less accepted"
- **Abstract says:** "may influence coworkers' evaluations... which are then associated with lower levels of coworkers' stress"
- **Problem:** The abstract uses hedged and associational language ("may influence", "associated with"); the digest states the effect as established fact.
- **Suggested fix:** "Soften to "an unreciprocated helping relationship is linked to more stress for the helper and less acceptance of the newcomer"."

### Study 10: Coping strategies that help women survive a male-dominated field can also entrench it
**Work ID:** W7204477379 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 11: Employees without children are quietly keeping score on your flexibility policies
**Work ID:** W7213900915 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Within-group variation dropped** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Parents valued flexibility when it came with managerial backing but some reported career penalties; employees childless by choice perceived inequity when parent-focused arrangements created extra availability demands on them without recognition"
- **Abstract says:** "Fairness perceptions varied both across and within family-status groups. ... Employees without children by choice perceived inequity when parent-centred arrangements generated additional availability expectations without corresponding recognition; more inclusive configurations were associated with favourable evaluations."
- **Problem:** The digest presents each family-status group as holding a single uniform view, whereas the abstract explicitly reports variation within groups and a positive configuration for the childless-by-choice group under inclusive arrangements. The paper's stated conclusion is that family status does not uniformly determine fairness judgments.
- **Suggested fix:** "Add a clause such as "views varied within groups too — childless-by-choice employees judged more inclusive arrangements favourably"."

### Study 12: "Nowhereness": when neither work nor home is a safe place to be yourself
**Work ID:** W7213532045 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 13: A two-minute allocation game predicts which job perks candidates actually care about
**Work ID:** W7204088664 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Invented task duration** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "A two-minute allocation game predicts which job perks candidates actually care about"
- **Abstract says:** "Social Value Orientation (SVO), assessed via a behavioral resource-allocation instrument (i.e., the SVO slider measure)"
- **Problem:** The abstract gives no administration time for the SVO Slider, so "two-minute" is a specific detail not supported by the source.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop the duration: "A short allocation game predicts which job perks candidates say they care about"."

**Issue B. Null result read as universal appeal** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "perks that benefit employees directly attract everyone regardless of values"
- **Abstract says:** "showing no significant association with employee CSR, consistent with the direct personal benefits it confers on employees"
- **Problem:** A non-significant association between SVO and employee-CSR importance means prosocial values did not predict that preference; it does not establish that employee-focused CSR "attracts everyone."
- **Suggested fix:** "Rephrase to "employee-focused CSR was valued similarly regardless of participants' prosocial values.""

### Study 14: Free tuition beats reimbursement: how education perks keep frontline workers from quitting
**Work ID:** W7211872890 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Causal headline for correlational/intentions evidence** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Free tuition beats reimbursement: how education perks keep frontline workers from quitting"
- **Abstract says:** "program participation is associated with reduced turnover ... educational benefits with little to no upfront costs—termed tuition assistance programs—are more strongly associated with reduced turnover intentions"
- **Problem:** The headline asserts that the benefit keeps workers from quitting, while Study 1 is an association and the design comparison rests on vignette-measured turnover intentions. The body and caveats hedge correctly, so only the headline overreaches. "Free tuition" also overstates "little to no upfront costs."
- **Suggested fix:** "Try "Up-front tuition support, not reimbursement: the education perk linked to lower quit intentions"."

### Study 15: That jokey job ad may be costing you candidates
**Work ID:** W7203608858 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 16: VR hiring tests make employers look more attractive — mainly to younger candidates
**Work ID:** W7202387608 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 17: A daily reflection prompt helped paramedics find meaning in bad shifts — but didn't move mental health symptoms
**Work ID:** W4412125794 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Country not stated in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "A randomized controlled pilot trial enrolled 83 emergency medical service clinicians in the US (89% White, 51% male)"
- **Abstract says:** "83/126 workers were eligible and randomized to intervention (n = 37) or control groups (n = 46). Most were White (89%) and male (51%)."
- **Problem:** The abstract does not name a country, so the US location is unverifiable from the abstract alone (the caveat repeats the same unverified claim).
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "emergency medical service clinicians (89% White, 51% male)" or attribute the location to the full paper."

**Issue B. "Paramedics" for EMS clinicians** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "A daily reflection prompt helped paramedics find meaning in bad shifts"
- **Abstract says:** "emergency medical service clinicians"
- **Problem:** "EMS clinicians" covers EMTs and other roles as well as paramedics, so the headline narrows the occupation slightly.
- **Suggested fix:** "Use "EMS clinicians" or "ambulance crews" in the headline."

### Study 18: What employees with ADHD say actually helps at work: informal relationships and flexible bosses
**Work ID:** W7208704204 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Unsupported comparative claim** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The relational environment, more than the work itself, shaped whether participants felt able to use their strengths."
- **Abstract says:** "this study examines how work relationships (i.e., socio-structural factors) enhance or hinder self-efficacy and goal attainment"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports that work relationships facilitate or hinder thriving; it makes no comparison against the nature of the work itself. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop the comparison: "Participants described the relational environment as decisive in whether they could use their strengths.""

**Issue B. Retention claim contradicted by own caveat** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "these workers point to everyday relational conditions — flexibility and approachable managers — as what determines whether they thrive or leave"
- **Abstract says:** "it examines neurodivergent employees' lived experiences of workplace relationships and investigates how these relationships facilitate or hinder their ability to thrive at work"
- **Problem:** The study measured no turnover outcome; the digest's caveat states the findings "cannot establish effects on performance or retention," so the body text contradicts the caveat by presenting relational conditions as determining whether people leave.
- **Suggested fix:** "Cut "or leave" and keep the claim to thriving at work as described by participants."

## Issue Summary

| Study # | Headline | Verdict | Notes |
|---------|----------|---------|-------|
| 1 | Hiring filters cut the applicant pool — and screen out the best candidates too | ⚠️ Minor issues | All headline numbers match the abstract and the randomized design supports causal language; one theorized mechanism is presented as an established result. |
| 2 | You can't have all three: the recruiting math that forces a trade-off between diversity, fairness and performance | ✅ Accurate | Design, six attraction scenarios, three outcomes and the paradox are all reported faithfully; caveats correctly flag the simulation-only basis. |
| 3 | Startup stock options attract engineers mostly as a signal, not as a financial bet | ✅ Accurate | Matches the abstract's series of experiments, the partial financial mediation, the symbolic inference about how the startup treats employees, and the prompting result; caveats appropriately note undisclosed sample details. |
| 4 | Rejected by an algorithm? Adding a human reviewer changes how candidates feel about you | ⚠️ Minor issues | Two mixed-methods studies, four profiles and the human-review effect are accurate; the attribution mechanism is proposed rather than clearly reported as a result. |
| 5 | Older and younger candidates talk differently in AI video interviews — and rewording the question narrows the gap | ✅ Accurate | Two studies, age range, control variables, and the Study 2 LLM-persona prompt test are all reported correctly, with appropriate caveats about simulated personas and unmeasured scoring consequences. |
| 6 | When a career ends against your will, work doesn't always matter less afterwards | ✅ Accurate | N=16, three interview waves, three patterns and five processes all match; caveats appropriately note the small interpretive sample. |
| 7 | What your LinkedIn profile says about your faith may be shaping who gets the interview | ⚠️ Minor issues | Design, both sample sizes and the similarity–liking mediation match; the stated direction of the moderator effects goes slightly beyond the abstract. |
| 8 | Applicants have had ChatGPT for years. Pre-employment test scores barely budged | ⚠️ Minor issues | Archival design, assessment mix and near-zero, inconsistent effects are accurate; the specific claim about younger applicants is not reported in the abstract. |
| 9 | Helping the new hire only pays off for you if they're good at the job | ⚠️ Minor issues | Two-study design and the reciprocity interaction are correct, but the mediation chain is flattened and the takeaway is stated more causally than the abstract's hedged wording. |
| 10 | Coping strategies that help women survive a male-dominated field can also entrench it | ✅ Accurate | Interview count, mixed-gender sample, occupational context and the survival-versus-change contrast all match the abstract; caveats correctly note the interpretive, single-occupation basis. |
| 11 | Employees without children are quietly keeping score on your flexibility policies | ⚠️ Minor issues | Design, N (65 interviews), single Big Four firm, fsQCA and the three family-status groups are all reported correctly. One nuance dropped: the abstract stresses that fairness perceptions varied within as well as across groups, and that more inclusive configurations drew favourable evaluations from the childless-by-choice group. |
| 12 | "Nowhereness": when neither work nor home is a safe place to be yourself | ✅ Accurate | Sample (29 gay men in various Indian organizations), qualitative interview design, the named stressors, bi-directional spillover and the "nowhereness" concept all match the abstract. Caveats appropriately limit generalizability; the managerial angle is framed as an implication rather than a finding. |
| 13 | A two-minute allocation game predicts which job perks candidates actually care about | ⚠️ Minor issues | N = 425 undergraduates, the SVO Slider, the adaptive choice-based conjoint attributes, salary dominance, employee CSR second, positive SVO links to environmental/social CSR, null for employee CSR and negative for salary are all faithful. Only the headline's invented "two-minute" detail and a slightly broad reading of the null need attention. |
| 14 | Free tuition beats reimbursement: how education perks keep frontline workers from quitting | ⚠️ Minor issues | Study 1's correlational turnover link, the two between-person vignette experiments, the perceived-organizational-support-for-development mechanism, the internal-career-opportunities moderator and the persistence across social classes and skill levels are all reported correctly, and the caveats are candid. The headline is more causal than the evidence. |
| 15 | That jokey job ad may be costing you candidates | ✅ Accurate | Three experiments, the single-stimulus vs. stimulus-sampling contrast, the negative attractiveness effect in Studies 1-2 and null in Study 3, and the consistent procedural-justice expectation effect all match the abstract. Caveats appropriately flag the inconsistency and the simulated-posting design. |
| 16 | VR hiring tests make employers look more attractive — mainly to younger candidates | ✅ Accurate | Sample sizes (122, 121), the video-vs-text and VR-vs-text comparisons, presence mediation for VR, the null attractiveness effect for video, and the weaker VR effect among older test-takers are all reported accurately, with the separate-studies limitation noted in caveats. |
| 17 | A daily reflection prompt helped paramedics find meaning in bad shifts — but didn't move mental health symptoms | ⚠️ Minor issues | Randomization, N=83 (37/46), demographics, eight daily assessments, 10 reflection prompts, the meaning-made effect and its growth across days, the adherence/fidelity pattern and the null results on other mechanisms and mental health outcomes all match. Only the stated country and the "paramedics" shorthand go slightly beyond the abstract. |
| 18 | What employees with ADHD say actually helps at work: informal relationships and flexible bosses | ⚠️ Minor issues | Recruitment via private psychotherapy practices in Italy, the interpretive qualitative design and the four themes are reported accurately. Two interpretive additions go beyond the abstract: a comparative claim about relationships mattering more than the work itself, and a "thrive or leave" outcome claim that the digest's own caveat disowns. |

**Total issues:** 15 (14 Minor, 1 Moderate, 0 Major)
**Entries requiring revision:** 10
**Entries cleared:** 8
